flawed_step: Lines 60–64 incorrectly infer that S has no neighbors in W_m merely because R_{m-1} ⊆ S and R_{m-1} has no neighbors in W_m. The vertices added to form S may have such neighbors.
counterexample: Let n=6 and α=1/6. Take G to be a K5 on vertices {a,b,c,d,e} plus an isolated vertex r. This satisfies the expansion hypothesis: every 3-vertex set has at least 4 neighbors (indeed, either 5 or at least 4). Let W_m={a,b,c,d,e}, W_{m-1}={r,a,b,c,d}, and R_{m-1}={r}. Both W-sets have the required size 5. Although R_{m-1} has no neighbor in W_m, extending it to S={r,a,b}, of size n/2=3, introduces neighbors in W_m; for example, a is adjacent to b. Thus N(S) is not contained in V\W_m.
assessment_summary: The central contradiction fails because the half-sized extension of the reachable set need not preserve its lack of edges to the next layer.
